decks.title: Mensuration — Part 1: Cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere
goals: Find the curved and total surface area and the volume of a solid or hollow cylinder
Find the slant height, surface areas and volume of a cone
Find the surface area and volume of a sphere, a hemisphere and a spherical shell
Choose the right formula and give the answer in square or cubic units

slides.heading: Cylinder, cone and sphere
slides.body_md: Tins, funnels and footballs are all **solids**. In this part we find how much **surface** they have and how much they **hold**, using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ where the question says so.

visual.alt: A solid right circular cylinder standing on its base. The radius r is marked along the top face and the height h on the right.
visual.caption: A cylinder: radius $r$, height $h$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Welcome to mensuration. A tin, a funnel and a football are solids. For each we want two things: the area of its surface, which tells us how much paint or paper it needs, and its volume, which tells us how much it can hold. In this part we study the cylinder, the cone, the sphere and the hemisphere.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the formulas for a **cylinder**, solid or hollow
Find the **slant height** and the areas and volume of a **cone**
Use the formulas for a **sphere**, a **hemisphere** and a **shell**
Write answers in **square or cubic** units

visual.alt: Table of the formulas for a solid cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere: the curved surface area, the total surface area and the volume of each.
visual.caption: The formulas of this chapter on one card.

slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. We use the formulas for solid and hollow cylinders, find the slant height of a cone, and use the formulas for spheres, hemispheres and spherical shells. The table shows every formula of this part on one card. Part two applies them to cost problems, melting and combinations of solids.

slides.heading: The cylinder and its curved surface
slides.body_md: A **right circular cylinder** has two equal circular ends and a curved surface. Cut the curved surface along a line and unroll it: it becomes a **rectangle** whose length is the circumference $2\pi r$ and whose width is the height $h$.

visual.alt: The net of a cylinder: a rectangle whose length is the circumference 2 pi r of the base and whose width is the height h, with a circle above and a circle below for the two ends.
visual.caption: The curved surface unrolls into a rectangle $2\pi r$ by $h$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: A right circular cylinder has two equal circular ends and one curved surface. Cut the curved surface along a line and unroll it. It becomes a rectangle. Its length is the distance round the circle, two pi r, and its width is the height h. So the curved surface area is two pi r times h. The two circular ends add two times pi r squared.

slides.heading: Cylinder: three formulas
slides.body_md: For a solid cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$:
bullets: an **open** tank has no top: curved surface $+$ **one** base
areas are in square units, volume in cubic units

visual.alt: A solid right circular cylinder standing on its base. The radius r is marked along the top face and the height h on the right.
visual.caption: A cylinder: radius $r$, height $h$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Here are the three formulas for a cylinder of radius r and height h. The curved surface area is two pi r h. The total surface area adds both ends and is two pi r times r plus h. The volume is pi r squared h. For an open tank there is no top, so use the curved surface plus one base only.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a closed tin
slides.body_md: A closed cylindrical tin has radius $10.5$ cm and height $20$ cm. Find its curved surface area, total surface area and volume. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

visual.alt: A closed solid cylinder, the tin of worked example 1, with the base radius 10.5 cm marked along the top and the height 20 cm on the right.
visual.caption: The tin (not to scale).

slides.narration: The tin has radius ten point five centimetres and height twenty centimetres. The curved surface is two pi r h, which is one thousand three hundred and twenty square centimetres. The total surface uses two pi r times r plus h and comes to two thousand and thirteen square centimetres. The volume is pi r squared h, which is six thousand nine hundred and thirty cubic centimetres. Areas are square units and volumes are cubic units.

slides.heading: Quick check: curved surface of a cylinder
slides.body_md: Which formula is the curved surface only?

visual.alt: The net of a cylinder: a rectangle whose length is the circumference 2 pi r of the base and whose width is the height h, with a circle above and a circle below for the two ends.
visual.caption: The curved surface unrolls into a rectangle $2\pi r$ by $h$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Which formula gives only the curved surface of a cylinder? Remember that the curved surface unrolls into a rectangle, and think about which formulas include the circular ends and which one is the volume.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an open tank
slides.body_md: An open cylindrical tank has inner radius $1.4$ m and depth $3.5$ m. Find its capacity in litres and the area of sheet needed to make it ($1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres, $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
bullets: **Step 3 —** sheet = curved surface $+$ one base: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1.4 \times 3.5 = 30.8$ m$^2$ and $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 1.4^2 = 6.16$ m$^2$

visual.alt: An open cylindrical tank, worked example 2, with the inner radius 1.4 m along the open top and the depth 3.5 m on the right.
visual.caption: The tank is open at the top (not to scale).

slides.narration: The tank has radius one point four metres and depth three point five metres. Its volume is twenty one point five six cubic metres, and one cubic metre is one thousand litres, so it holds twenty one thousand five hundred and sixty litres. The sheet needed is the curved surface, thirty point eight square metres, plus one base, six point one six square metres, because the top is open. That makes thirty six point nine six square metres.

slides.heading: The hollow cylinder
slides.body_md: A **hollow cylinder**, such as a pipe, has an outer radius $R$ and an inner radius $r$. The **metal** is the outer cylinder with the bore taken away.
bullets: curved surfaces: outside $2\pi R h$, inside $2\pi r h$
thickness $= R - r$; find $r$ from the thickness first when needed

visual.alt: A hollow cylinder, like a pipe: the outer radius R and the inner radius r are marked on the top ring and the length h on the right, with the bore shown by dashed lines.
visual.caption: Hollow cylinder: outer radius $R$, inner radius $r$, length $h$ (not to scale).

math: V_{\text{metal}} = \pi R^2 h - \pi r^2 h = \pi h(R^2 - r^2)
slides.narration: A hollow cylinder, such as a pipe, has an outer radius capital R and an inner radius small r. The metal is the outer cylinder with the bore taken away, so its volume is pi h times R squared minus r squared. The outside curved surface is two pi R h and the inside curved surface is two pi r h. If you are given the thickness, subtract it from R to find r.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a metal pipe
slides.body_md: A metal pipe is $14$ cm long with outer radius $6$ cm and inner radius $5$ cm. Find the volume of metal and the area of its outer and inner curved surfaces. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

visual.alt: A metal pipe, worked example 3: outer radius 6 cm and inner radius 5 cm on the top ring, length 14 cm on the right.
visual.caption: The pipe (not to scale).

slides.narration: The pipe is fourteen centimetres long, with outer radius six and inner radius five. The metal has volume pi times fourteen times the difference between thirty six and twenty five, which comes to four hundred and eighty four cubic centimetres. The outside curved surface is five hundred and twenty eight square centimetres and the inside is four hundred and forty. Together the two curved surfaces measure nine hundred and sixty eight square centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: doubling a cylinder
slides.body_md: Both the radius and the height are doubled.

visual.alt: A solid right circular cylinder standing on its base. The radius r is marked along the top face and the height h on the right.
visual.caption: A cylinder: radius $r$, height $h$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Here is a true or false question. Both the radius and the height of a cylinder are doubled. Think about what happens to the curved surface area, which is two pi r h, when both r and h become twice as large.

slides.heading: The cone and its slant height
slides.body_md: A **right circular cone** has a circular base, an apex and a curved surface. The **vertical height** $h$, the **radius** $r$ and the **slant height** $l$ form a right-angled triangle, so
bullets: $l$ is the length along the slope from the apex to the rim
always find $l$ first when it is not given

visual.alt: A right circular cone standing on its circular base. The vertical height h runs along the dashed axis, the radius r along the base and the slant height l along the sloping side.
visual.caption: A cone: radius $r$, height $h$, slant height $l$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: A right circular cone has a circular base and a pointed top called the apex. The vertical height, the radius and the slant height make a right angled triangle, with the slant height as the longest side. By Pythagoras, l squared is r squared plus h squared. The slant height is measured along the slope from the apex to the rim of the base.

slides.heading: Cone: the formulas
slides.body_md: The curved surface of a cone unrolls into part of a circle, and its area is $\pi r l$. The base adds $\pi r^2$. The volume is **one third** of the cylinder with the same base and height.

visual.alt: Table for a cone: slant height, curved surface area, total surface area and volume with the formulas and the values for radius 7 and height 24.
visual.caption: The cone formulas with one set of numbers.

math: \text{curved} = \pi r l, \quad \text{total} = \pi r(r + l), \quad V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h
slides.narration: The curved surface area of a cone is pi r l, using the slant height. The total surface area adds the circular base and is pi r times r plus l. The volume is one third of pi r squared h, exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height. The table shows a cone with radius seven and height twenty four, whose slant height is twenty five.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a cone
slides.body_md: A cone has radius $10.5$ cm and vertical height $14$ cm. Find the slant height, the curved surface area, the total surface area and the volume ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

visual.alt: The cone of worked example 4, with radius 10.5 cm, vertical height 14 cm and slant height 17.5 cm marked.
visual.caption: The cone (not to scale).

slides.narration: The cone has radius ten point five and height fourteen. First the slant height: the square root of one hundred and ten point two five plus one hundred and ninety six is the square root of three hundred and six point two five, which is seventeen point five. The curved surface is five hundred and seventy seven point five square centimetres, the total surface is nine hundred and twenty four square centimetres, and the volume is one thousand six hundred and seventeen cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: from the curved area back to the height
slides.body_md: The curved surface area of a cone is $2310$ cm$^2$ and its base radius is $21$ cm. Find the slant height, the vertical height and the volume ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

visual.alt: The cone of worked example 5 with the radius 21 cm and the slant height 35 cm known; the vertical height h is to be found.
visual.caption: The cone: find $h$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: The curved surface area is two thousand three hundred and ten and the radius is twenty one. Pi r l equals two thousand three hundred and ten, and pi times twenty one is sixty six, so the slant height is two thousand three hundred and ten divided by sixty six, which is thirty five. Then the height is the square root of seven hundred and eighty four, which is twenty eight. The volume is twelve thousand nine hundred and thirty six cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: the slant height
slides.body_md: Which formula gives $l$?

visual.alt: A right circular cone standing on its circular base. The vertical height h runs along the dashed axis, the radius r along the base and the slant height l along the sloping side.
visual.caption: A cone: radius $r$, height $h$, slant height $l$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Which formula gives the slant height of a cone? Remember the right angled triangle formed by the radius, the height and the slope, and that the slope is its longest side.

slides.heading: The sphere
slides.body_md: Every point of a **sphere** is the same distance $r$ from its centre. Its surface is all curved.
bullets: the surface area is **four times** the area of a great circle
a diameter $d$ gives $r = \dfrac{d}{2}$: halve before using the formula

visual.alt: A sphere with its centre, an equator drawn as an ellipse with the hidden half dashed, and a radius r marked to the surface.
visual.caption: A sphere of radius $r$.

slides.narration: Every point of a sphere is the same distance r from the centre. Its surface area is four pi r squared, which is four times the area of a great circle. Its volume is four thirds pi r cubed. If the diameter is given, halve it first to get the radius before you use either formula.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a sphere
slides.body_md: A solid sphere has radius $21$ cm. Find its surface area and its volume ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

visual.alt: The sphere of worked example 6 with its radius of 21 cm marked from the centre to the surface.
visual.caption: The sphere (not to scale).

slides.narration: The sphere has radius twenty one centimetres. The surface area is four pi r squared, which is five thousand five hundred and forty four square centimetres. The volume is four thirds pi r cubed, and because twenty one is a multiple of seven the fractions cancel neatly, giving thirty eight thousand eight hundred and eight cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: The hemisphere
slides.body_md: Cut a sphere through its centre: each half is a **hemisphere**. A **solid** hemisphere has a curved surface and a flat circular face.
bullets: a hollow **bowl** is open at the top, so only the curved surface is counted

visual.alt: A solid hemisphere with its flat circular face at the bottom drawn as an ellipse, the dome above it, and the radius r marked on the flat face.
visual.caption: A solid hemisphere: curved surface $2\pi r^2$, flat face $\pi r^2$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Cut a sphere through its centre and each half is a hemisphere. The curved surface is half of four pi r squared, which is two pi r squared. A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face of area pi r squared, so its total surface area is three pi r squared. The volume is two thirds pi r cubed. An open bowl has only the curved surface.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a solid hemisphere
slides.body_md: A solid hemisphere has radius $21$ cm. Find its curved surface area, total surface area and volume ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

visual.alt: The solid hemisphere of worked example 7 with its radius of 21 cm marked on the flat face.
visual.caption: The solid hemisphere (not to scale).

slides.narration: The hemisphere has radius twenty one. The curved surface is two thousand seven hundred and seventy two square centimetres. The total surface, including the flat face, is four thousand one hundred and fifty eight square centimetres, which is three halves of the curved part. The volume is nineteen thousand four hundred and four cubic centimetres, exactly half of the volume of the whole sphere of the same radius.

slides.heading: Quick check: whole surface of a hemisphere
slides.body_md: Count the flat face as well.

visual.alt: A solid hemisphere with its flat circular face at the bottom drawn as an ellipse, the dome above it, and the radius r marked on the flat face.
visual.caption: A solid hemisphere: curved surface $2\pi r^2$, flat face $\pi r^2$ (not to scale).

slides.narration: Which formula gives the total surface area of a solid hemisphere? A solid hemisphere has a curved surface and one flat circular face, so decide which areas to add.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a hollow sphere
slides.body_md: A hollow metal sphere has outer radius $5.5$ cm and inner radius $4$ cm. Find the volume of metal ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
bullets: **Step 2 —** here $5.5^3 = 166.375$ and $4^3 = 64$, so the difference is $102.375$

visual.alt: The hollow metal sphere of worked example 8 in cross-section, with the outer radius 5.5 cm and the inner radius 4 cm marked.
visual.caption: The hollow sphere in section (not to scale).

slides.narration: A hollow sphere has outer radius five point five and inner radius four. The metal is the outer sphere with the inner sphere taken away, so its volume is four thirds pi times the difference of the cubes of the radii. The cubes are one hundred and sixty six point three seven five and sixty four, with difference one hundred and two point three seven five. The volume of metal is four hundred and twenty nine cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cylinder: $2\pi r h$, $2\pi r(r + h)$, $\pi r^2 h$
Cone: find $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$; $\pi r l$, $\pi r(r + l)$, $\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
Sphere: $4\pi r^2$ and $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$; hemisphere: $2\pi r^2$, $3\pi r^2$, $\dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3$

rows: $2\pi r(r + h)$; $\pi r^2 h$ for volume
$2\pi R h$ outside, $2\pi r h$ inside

visual.alt: Summary table for part 1: which formula to use for the curved surface and for the whole surface or volume of a cylinder, hollow cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A cylinder has curved surface two pi r h and volume pi r squared h. A hollow cylinder has metal volume pi h times R squared minus r squared. For a cone find the slant height first. A sphere has surface four pi r squared and volume four thirds pi r cubed. A hemisphere has curved surface two pi r squared and total surface three pi r squared.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Formula (1 mark):** write it before you substitute
**Working (1–2 marks):** the slant height or the inner radius first, then the substitution
**Answer (1 mark):** with **cm$^2$** for areas and **cm$^3$** for volumes
**Mistake:** using the diameter as the radius
**Mistake:** using the height instead of the slant height in $\pi r l$
**Mistake:** counting a top that an open tank or a bowl does not have

rows: Working, with the slant height or radius found first

visual.alt: Table of how marks are usually awarded in a mensuration question: the formula, the working and the final answer with its unit.
visual.caption: A typical mark split for a 3 or 4 mark part.

slides.narration: In the exam, write the formula first, then substitute. Find the slant height or the inner radius before the main calculation. State the answer with square units for areas and cubic units for volumes. Common slips are using the diameter as the radius, using the height instead of the slant height, and counting a top that an open tank or a bowl does not have.

decks.title: Mensuration — Part 2: Cost problems, melting and recasting, combinations of solids
goals: Find the cost of painting a surface or filling a container from its area or volume
Find the volume of the material in a hollow solid from its outer and inner volumes
Use equality of volume to find the number or dimensions of solids formed by melting and recasting
Find the surface area and volume of a solid made of a cylinder, a cone and a hemisphere

slides.heading: Cost, melting and combinations
slides.body_md: In part 2 the formulas go to work: **how much will it cost** to paint or fill a solid, **what comes out** when a solid is melted and recast, and what happens when solids are **joined**.

visual.alt: Flow chart of melting and recasting: a solid A is melted and recast into a solid B, and the volume of A equals the volume of B.
visual.caption: Melting and recasting changes the shape, not the volume.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Now the formulas go to work. How much does it cost to paint a dome or fill a tank? What do we get when a metal solid is melted and recast into another shape? And how do we handle a solid made by joining a cylinder, a cone and a hemisphere? The key idea in recasting is that the volume does not change.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **cost** of painting, polishing or filling
Find the metal in a **hollow** solid: inner and outer volume
Use **equal volumes** for melting and recasting
Handle **combinations** of a cylinder, cone and hemisphere

rows: using volume, or the wrong surfaces
forgetting to convert cubic metres to litres
using the thickness as the radius
areas of the outside surfaces; volumes added

visual.alt: Summary table for part 2: cost of painting uses area, cost of filling uses litres, hollow solids use outer minus inner volume, melting keeps the volume, and combinations hide the joined faces.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We find the cost of painting, polishing or filling. We find the metal in a hollow solid from its inner and outer volumes. We use equal volumes for melting and recasting. And we work with solids made of a cylinder, a cone and a hemisphere joined together. The table gives each rule in one line.

slides.heading: Units first
slides.body_md: Costs are given **per square unit** or **per litre**. Convert **before** you multiply, so that the units of the quantity and the rate match.
bullets: a tank in cubic metres is filled in **litres**: multiply by $1000$
a radius in cm and a rate per m$^2$ need one common unit

visual.alt: Table of unit conversions used in mensuration cost problems: cubic metres to litres, litres to cubic centimetres, metres to centimetres, square metres to square centimetres.
visual.caption: Convert before you multiply by a rate.

slides.narration: Costs are given per square unit or per litre, so convert before you multiply. One cubic metre is one thousand litres. One litre is one thousand cubic centimetres. One metre is one hundred centimetres, and one square metre is ten thousand square centimetres. Always make the unit of the quantity match the unit of the rate.

slides.heading: Which quantity does the rate need?
slides.body_md: Ask what the rate is **per**. A rate per **square metre** needs a surface area; a rate per **litre** needs a volume.
bullets: filling, water, oil, fuel: **volume** in litres
only the surfaces that are really painted: an open tank has no top

nodes.label: What does the rate apply to?
Painting, polishing, plating, canvas: find an area, then area × rate per square unit
Filling, fuel, water: find a volume, convert to litres, then litres × rate per litre

visual.alt: Flow chart for cost problems: if the rate is per square unit find the surface area and multiply by the rate; if the rate is per litre find the volume, convert to litres and multiply by the rate.
visual.caption: Match the rate to the quantity.

slides.narration: Ask what the rate is per. A rate per square metre needs a surface area, as for painting, polishing, plating or canvas. A rate per litre needs a volume converted to litres, as for water, oil or fuel. And count only the surfaces that are really painted: an open tank has no top, and the ground under a dome is not painted.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: painting a dome
slides.body_md: The hemispherical dome of a hall has radius $14$ m. Find the cost of painting its outside at ₹ $15$ per m$^2$ ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
bullets: **Step 1 —** a dome has only its curved surface: $S = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 1232$ m$^2$

visual.alt: A hemispherical dome standing on a flat circular base, the radius of 14 m marked on the base, for worked example 1.
visual.caption: The dome (not to scale).

slides.narration: The dome is a hemisphere of radius fourteen metres. Only the curved surface is painted, and it is two pi r squared, which is one thousand two hundred and thirty two square metres. At fifteen rupees for each square metre the cost is one thousand two hundred and thirty two times fifteen, which is eighteen thousand four hundred and eighty rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: filling a drum
slides.body_md: A closed cylindrical drum has radius $0.35$ m and height $1.2$ m. Cooking oil costs ₹ $85$ per litre. Find the cost of filling the drum ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

visual.alt: A closed cylindrical oil drum with the radius 0.35 m marked along the top and the height 1.2 m on the right, for worked example 2.
visual.caption: The oil drum (not to scale).

slides.narration: The drum has radius zero point three five metres and height one point two metres. Its volume is zero point four six two cubic metres. That is four hundred and sixty two litres. At eighty five rupees a litre, the cost is four hundred and sixty two times eighty five, which is thirty nine thousand two hundred and seventy rupees. The rate is per litre, so we used the volume.

slides.heading: Quick check: cubic metres to litres
slides.body_md: Convert before pricing.

visual.alt: Table of unit conversions used in mensuration cost problems: cubic metres to litres, litres to cubic centimetres, metres to centimetres, square metres to square centimetres.
visual.caption: Convert before you multiply by a rate.

slides.narration: A rainwater tank holds six point six cubic metres. Convert this to litres. Remember how many litres make one cubic metre.

slides.heading: Inner and outer volume
slides.body_md: A **hollow** solid is an outer solid with an inner space taken out. The material it is made of has volume
bullets: the **capacity** of a vessel is its **inner** volume

visual.alt: A cross-section of a thick hollow solid drawn as two circles with the same centre: the outer radius R and the inner radius r are marked, and the metal lies between them.
visual.caption: Metal $=$ outer volume $-$ inner volume (not to scale).

slides.narration: A hollow solid is an outer solid with an inner space taken out. The material it is made of has volume equal to the outer volume minus the inner volume. The mass of the material is its volume times the mass of one cubic centimetre. The capacity of a vessel, how much it can hold, is its inner volume, not the outer volume.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a metal bowl
slides.body_md: A hemispherical bowl of steel has outer radius $6.5$ cm and inner radius $5$ cm. Find the volume of steel and its mass, if $1$ cm$^3$ of steel has a mass of $8$ g ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

visual.alt: A hemispherical metal bowl open at the top with its outer radius of 6.5 cm marked; the inner radius is 5 cm, for worked example 3.
visual.caption: The bowl: outer radius $6.5$ cm, inner radius $5$ cm (not to scale).

slides.narration: The bowl is a hemisphere of outer radius six point five and inner radius five. The steel is the outer hemisphere minus the inner one, two thirds pi times the difference of the cubes, which is three hundred and thirteen point five cubic centimetres. Each cubic centimetre has a mass of eight grams, so the bowl has a mass of two thousand five hundred and eight grams, which is two point five zero eight kilograms.

slides.heading: Melting and recasting
slides.body_md: When a solid is **melted and recast**, no material is gained or lost, so the **volume stays the same**. The shape, the surface area and the dimensions all change.
bullets: one solid into $n$ equal solids: $V = n \times v$

visual.alt: Flow chart of melting and recasting: a solid A is melted and recast into a solid B, and the volume of A equals the volume of B.
visual.caption: Melting and recasting changes the shape, not the volume.

slides.narration: When a solid is melted and recast, no material is gained or lost, so the volume stays the same. The shape changes, and so do the surface area and the dimensions. If one solid becomes n equal solids, the volume of the first equals n times the volume of one new solid. The common factor pi, and often four thirds, cancels from both sides.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: one sphere into many
slides.body_md: A solid sphere of radius $7.5$ cm is melted and recast into small solid spheres of radius $1.5$ cm. How many are made?
bullets: **Check —** the radius is $5$ times as large, so the volume is $5^3 = 125$ times as large

visual.alt: Flow chart for worked example 4: one sphere of radius 7.5 centimetres is melted and recast into n small spheres of radius 1.5 centimetres.
visual.caption: Volume of 1 big sphere $= n \times$ volume of 1 small sphere.

slides.narration: A sphere of radius seven point five is melted and recast into small spheres of radius one point five. Equal volumes give n times four thirds pi times one point five cubed equal to four thirds pi times seven point five cubed. The common factor cancels, and n is the ratio of the cubes, four hundred and twenty one point eight seven five divided by three point three seven five, which is one hundred and twenty five.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a rod drawn into wire
slides.body_md: A solid copper rod of radius $1.4$ cm and length $25$ cm is drawn into a uniform wire of radius $0.1$ cm. Find the length of the wire in metres.

visual.alt: A thin solid copper rod, a cylinder of radius 1.4 cm and length 25 cm, which is drawn into a longer thinner wire in worked example 5.
visual.caption: The copper rod (not to scale).

slides.narration: The rod is a cylinder of radius one point four centimetres and length twenty five. Its volume is pi times one point nine six times twenty five, which is forty nine pi. The wire is a long thin cylinder of radius zero point one, with volume pi times zero point zero one times its length. Equal volumes give a length of four thousand nine hundred centimetres, which is forty nine metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: cylinder recast as a cone
slides.body_md: Same volume, same base radius.

visual.alt: The cone in worked example 6 with its base radius of 6 cm marked and its height h to be found; it is made by melting a hemisphere of radius 6 cm.
visual.caption: The new cone: find $h$ (not to scale).

sections.heading: 1. The cylinder
sections.body_md:
- A **right circular cylinder** of base radius $r$ and height $h$ has two circular ends and a curved surface; the curved surface unrolls into a rectangle $2\pi r$ by $h$.
- **Curved surface area** $= 2\pi r h$; **total surface area** $= 2\pi r(r + h)$; **volume** $= \pi r^2 h$.
- An **open** tank or can has no top: curved surface $+$ one base. A **closed** tin has both ends.
- Volumes are in cubic units: $1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres and $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm$^3$.

*Example:* a tin with $r = 10.5$ cm and $h = 20$ cm: $S = 1320$ cm$^2$, total $= 2013$ cm$^2$, $V = 6930$ cm$^3$ (using $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

key_terms.definition_md: The area of the curved face of a solid, without its flat ends.
The curved surface area plus the areas of the flat faces.
The volume of liquid a hollow container holds; $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm$^3$.

visual.alt: A solid right circular cylinder standing on its base. The radius r is marked along the top face and the height h on the right.
visual.caption: A cylinder: radius $r$, height $h$ (not to scale).

visuals.caption: The curved surface unrolls into a rectangle $2\pi r$ by $h$ (not to scale).

sections.heading: 2. The hollow cylinder
sections.body_md:
- A pipe or tube has outer radius $R$, inner radius $r$ and length $h$; the **thickness** is $R - r$.
- **Metal** $= \pi R^2 h - \pi r^2 h = \pi h(R^2 - r^2)$.
- Outside curved surface $2\pi R h$, inside curved surface $2\pi r h$, and two ring-shaped ends of area $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$ each.
- Always find $r$ from the thickness first when it is given instead of $r$.

*Example:* $R = 6$ cm, $r = 5$ cm, $h = 14$ cm: $V = 484$ cm$^3$; the two curved surfaces measure $528 + 440 = 968$ cm$^2$.

key_terms.definition_md: A cylinder with a cylindrical bore through it, such as a pipe; it has an outer and an inner radius.
The difference $R - r$ between the outer and inner radii.

visual.alt: A hollow cylinder, like a pipe: the outer radius R and the inner radius r are marked on the top ring and the length h on the right, with the bore shown by dashed lines.
visual.caption: Hollow cylinder: outer radius $R$, inner radius $r$, length $h$ (not to scale).

visuals.caption: The pipe (not to scale).

sections.heading: 3. The cone
sections.body_md:
- A **right circular cone** has base radius $r$, vertical height $h$ and **slant height** $l$ with $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$.
- **Curved surface** $= \pi r l$; **total surface** $= \pi r(r + l)$; **volume** $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$ (one third of the cylinder with the same base and height).
- Find $l$ first when only $r$ and $h$ are given; when the curved area is given, $l = \dfrac{\text{curved area}}{\pi r}$.
- Not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus: the frustum of a cone.

*Example:* $r = 10.5$ cm, $h = 14$ cm: $l = 17.5$ cm, curved $= 577.5$ cm$^2$, total $= 924$ cm$^2$, $V = 1617$ cm$^3$.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance along the sloping side of a cone from its apex to the rim of its base: $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$.
The pointed top of a cone.

visual.alt: A right circular cone standing on its circular base. The vertical height h runs along the dashed axis, the radius r along the base and the slant height l along the sloping side.

sections.heading: 4. The sphere and the hemisphere
sections.body_md:
- **Sphere:** surface area $4\pi r^2$ (four times a great circle), volume $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. Halve a diameter to get $r$.
- **Hemisphere:** curved surface $2\pi r^2$, total surface of a solid hemisphere $3\pi r^2$ (the flat face adds $\pi r^2$), volume $\dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3$.
- A hollow **bowl** is open at the top: only the curved surface is counted.

*Example:* a sphere of radius $21$ cm has $S = 5544$ cm$^2$ and $V = 38808$ cm$^3$; a solid hemisphere of the same radius has curved surface $2772$ cm$^2$, total $4158$ cm$^2$ and volume $19404$ cm$^3$.

key_terms.definition_md: Half of a sphere, cut by a plane through its centre.
The circle in which a plane through the centre cuts a sphere; its area is $\pi r^2$.

sections.heading: 5. Spherical shells; inner and outer volume
sections.body_md:
- A **spherical shell** (hollow sphere) of outer radius $R$ and inner radius $r$ has metal of volume $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi (R^3 - r^3)$; a hemispherical bowl has $\dfrac{2}{3}\pi (R^3 - r^3)$.
- **Material** $=$ outer volume $-$ inner volume; **capacity** $=$ inner volume.
- **Mass** $=$ volume $\times$ mass of $1$ cm$^3$ (density).

*Example:* $R = 5.5$ cm, $r = 4$ cm: $V = 429$ cm$^3$ of metal; a hemispherical bowl with $R = 6.5$ cm and $r = 5$ cm holds 313.5 cm$^3$ of steel, and its mass is $313.5 \times 8 = 2508$ g.

key_terms.definition_md: A hollow sphere: the material between two concentric spheres.
The mass of one unit of volume of a material, for example $8$ g per cm$^3$.

sections.heading: 6. Cost problems
sections.body_md:
- A rate **per square unit** (painting, polishing, plating, canvas) needs a **surface area**; a rate **per litre** (water, oil, fuel) needs a **volume** in litres.
- Convert first: $1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres, $1$ m $= 100$ cm, $1$ m$^2 = 10000$ cm$^2$.
- Count only the surfaces that are really painted: an open tank has no top, and the ground under a dome is not painted.

*Example:* a dome of radius $14$ m has curved surface $1232$ m$^2$; at ₹ $15$ per m$^2$ painting costs ₹ 18480. A drum holding $0.462$ m$^3$ holds $462$ litres, which cost ₹ 39270 at ₹ $85$ per litre.

sections.heading: 7. Melting and recasting
sections.body_md:
- When a solid is melted and recast, **volume before $=$ volume after**; surface area and dimensions change.
- One solid into $n$ equal solids: $V = n \times v$; the common factor $\pi$ (and often $\dfrac{4}{3}$) cancels, so $n$ is a ratio of cubes for spheres.
- A rod drawn into a wire: $\pi R^2 h = \pi r^2 l$, so $l = \dfrac{R^2 h}{r^2}$.
- A solid submerged in an upright cylinder raises the water by $x$ with $\pi R^2 x = V_{\text{solid}}$.

*Example:* a sphere of radius $7.5$ cm gives $125$ spheres of radius $1.5$ cm; a rod of radius $1.4$ cm and length $25$ cm becomes a wire of radius $0.1$ cm and length $49$ m; a hemisphere of radius $6$ cm becomes a cone of base radius $6$ cm and height $12$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: Melting a solid and forming a new solid of a different shape from the same material.
The volume of water pushed aside by a submerged solid; it equals the volume of the solid.

sections.heading: 8. Combinations of solids
sections.body_md:
- Add the **volumes** of the parts. For the **surface**, count only the faces on the **outside**: a joined face is hidden.
- A hemisphere, a cylinder and a cone of the same radius: outside area $=$ hemisphere $2\pi r^2$ $+$ cylinder $2\pi r h$ $+$ cone $\pi r l$ (find $l$ first).
- A hemisphere or cone hollowed out of a cylinder removes volume and may remove or add surface: check which faces remain.

*Example:* a cylinder with $r = 4.2$ cm and $h = 6$ cm under a cone of height $5.6$ cm ($l = 7$ cm): outside area $55.44 + 158.4 + 92.4 = 306.24$ cm$^2$ and volume $332.64 + 103.488 = 436.128$ cm$^3$.

key_terms.definition_md: A solid made by joining simple solids along faces; its volume is the sum of the volumes of the parts.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Surface area or volume of one solid (2 marks):* formula 1, substitution and result with unit 1.
- *Cone (3 marks):* slant height 1, formula with substitution 1, result with unit 1.
- *Cost problem (3–4 marks):* area or volume 1–2, conversion of units 1, cost 1.
- *Melting and recasting (3–4 marks):* statement "volume before $=$ volume after" 1, the two volumes 1–2, answer 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually $3 + 3 + 4$; show the formula for every solid.

**Common mistakes**
1. Using the diameter where the radius is needed.
2. Using the vertical height instead of the slant height in $\pi r l$.
3. Counting a top that an open tank or a bowl does not have, or counting joined faces in a combination.
4. Forgetting the factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ for a cone, or the factor $\dfrac{4}{3}$ or $\dfrac{2}{3}$ for a sphere or hemisphere.
5. Forgetting to convert cubic metres to litres or centimetres to metres before multiplying by a rate.
6. Equating surface areas instead of volumes when a solid is melted and recast.

cards.back_md: $\pi h(R^2 - r^2)$, the outer cylinder minus the bore.

cards.front_md: A pipe has $R = 6$ cm, $r = 5$ cm and length $14$ cm. Find the metal ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

Common slip with cylinders?
cards.back_md: Using the diameter as the radius, or counting a top that an open tank does not have.

cards.front_md: State the slant height of a cone.
cards.back_md: $l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$: the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle formed by $r$, $h$ and $l$.

cards.front_md: What are the curved surface area, total surface area and volume of a cone?
cards.back_md: $\pi r l$, $\pi r(r + l)$ and $\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.

cards.front_md: A cone has $r = 7$ cm and $h = 24$ cm. Find $l$ and the curved surface area ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
cards.back_md: $l = 25$ cm and $S = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 = 550$ cm$^2$.

cards.front_md: How does the volume of a cone compare with a cylinder of the same base and height?
cards.back_md: It is one third of it.

cards.front_md: The curved surface of a cone is $2310$ cm$^2$ and $r = 21$ cm. Find $l$ ($\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
Common slip with cones?

cards.front_md: State the surface area and volume of a sphere of radius $r$.
cards.back_md: $4\pi r^2$ and $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.

cards.front_md: How does the surface area of a sphere compare with a great circle?
cards.back_md: It is four times the area $\pi r^2$ of a great circle.

State the curved surface, total surface and volume of a solid hemisphere.
Why is the total surface of a solid hemisphere $3\pi r^2$?
cards.back_md: The curved part is $2\pi r^2$ and the flat circular face adds $\pi r^2$.

cards.back_md: Its inner volume: the amount it can hold.

cards.back_md: Per m$^2$ needs an area; per litre needs a volume converted to litres.

cards.back_md: Curved hemisphere $2\pi r^2$, curved cylinder $2\pi r h$ and curved cone $\pi r l$.

questions.stem_md: The curved surface area of a solid right circular cylinder with base radius $r$ and height $h$ is
questions.solution_md: Roll the curved surface out flat: it is a rectangle $2\pi r$ long and $h$ wide, so its area is $2\pi r h$. Option (b) is the volume and option (c) is the total surface area, which also includes the two circular ends.

questions.stem_md: A cylindrical steel drum at a dairy in Anand has base radius $14$ cm and height $30$ cm. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the area of its curved surface only is
questions.solution_md: $S = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 30 = 2640$ cm$^2$. Option (c) is the total surface area, because it adds the two ends; option (d) is $\pi r h$, which forgets the factor $2$; option (a) is the volume.

questions.stem_md: A cylindrical water tank at a school in Nashik has inner radius $3.5$ m and height $4$ m. One cubic metre holds $1000$ litres, which is one kilolitre. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the tank holds
questions.solution_md: $V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 3.5^2 \times 4 = 154$ m$^3$, which is $154$ kilolitres. Option (d) forgets to square the radius, option (a) squares the diameter $7$ instead of the radius, and option (b) is the curved surface area.

questions.stem_md: The radius of a cylindrical candle mould is doubled and its height is halved. Its volume becomes

options.text_md: the same as the original volume

questions.solution_md: $V = \pi r^2 h$. With $2r$ and $\dfrac{h}{2}$ we get $\pi (2r)^2 \dfrac{h}{2} = 2\pi r^2 h = 2V$. The square on the radius multiplies by $4$ and the halved height multiplies by $\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the volume is multiplied by $2$.

questions.stem_md: A hollow iron pipe is $14$ cm long. Its outer radius is $8$ cm and its inner radius is $6$ cm. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the volume of iron in the pipe is
questions.solution_md: Iron $=$ outer cylinder $-$ bore: $V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times (8^2 - 6^2) = 1232$ cm$^3$. Option (b) squares the thickness $8 - 6$ instead of subtracting the squares; option (c) is the volume of the solid outer cylinder; option (d) squares the sum of the radii.

questions.stem_md: A right circular cone has base radius $r$ and vertical height $h$. Its slant height $l$ is given by
questions.solution_md: The height, the radius and the slant height form a right-angled triangle with the slant height as hypotenuse, so $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$ by Pythagoras. A hypotenuse is shorter than the sum of the other two sides, which rules out option (c).

questions.stem_md: A conical party hat made in Indore has base radius $5$ cm and vertical height $12$ cm. Its curved surface area, in terms of $\pi$, is
questions.solution_md: $l = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$, so $S = \pi r l = \pi \times 5 \times 13 = 65\pi$ cm$^2$. Option (d) uses the height $12$ in place of the slant height, option (a) takes $l = r + h = 17$, and option (b) is the total surface area $\pi r (r + l)$.

questions.stem_md: A conical funnel used in a spice shop in Kochi has base radius $6$ cm and height $14$ cm. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the volume it can hold is
questions.solution_md: $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 6^2 \times 14 = 528$ cm$^3$. Option (a) leaves out the factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$, which gives the cylinder with the same base and height; options (b) and (c) use $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\dfrac{2}{3}$ in place of $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: A conical tent for a camp near Mussoorie has a base of diameter $7$ m and a vertical height of $12$ m. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the canvas needed for its sloping surface is
questions.solution_md: $r = 3.5$ and $l = \sqrt{3.5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{156.25} = 12.5$ m. Then $S = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 3.5 \times 12.5 = 137.5$ m$^2$. Option (b) uses the height $12$ as the slant height, option (c) takes the diameter $7$ as the radius, and option (d) adds the floor, which a tent roof does not need.

questions.stem_md: A solid hemisphere of radius $r$ has a curved surface and one flat circular face. Its total surface area is
questions.solution_md: The curved surface is half of a sphere, $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 4\pi r^2 = 2\pi r^2$, and the flat face adds $\pi r^2$, so the total is $3\pi r^2$. Option (c) forgets the flat face.

questions.stem_md: The football used by a school team in Raipur has a diameter of $21$ cm. Treating it as a sphere and taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the area of its surface is
questions.solution_md: $r = \dfrac{21}{2} = 10.5$, so $S = 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^2 = 1386$ cm$^2$. Option (d) puts the diameter $21$ in the formula as a radius, option (a) is the curved surface of a hemisphere, and option (b) is only the area of a great circle.

questions.stem_md: The surface area of a solid brass sphere is $5544$ cm$^2$. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, its radius is
questions.solution_md: $4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times r^2 = 5544$ gives $r^2 = 5544 \times \dfrac{7}{88} = 441$, so $r = 21$ cm. Option (a) stops at $r^2$, option (b) comes from using the area $\pi r^2$ of a great circle, and option (c) from using $2\pi r^2$ and forgetting the root.

questions.stem_md: Two solid iron spheres have radii in the ratio $2 : 3$. The ratio of their volumes is
questions.solution_md: The volume of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its radius, so the ratio is $2^3 : 3^3 = 8 : 27$. Option (c) is the ratio of the surface areas, which depend on the square of the radius.

questions.stem_md: A round pillar outside a temple hall has a diameter of $84$ cm and a height of $3$ m. Its curved surface is to be painted at ₹ $25$ per m$^2$. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the cost of painting is
questions.solution_md: In metres $r = 0.42$ and $h = 3$. Area $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.42 \times 3 = 7.92$ m$^2$, and the cost is $7.92 \times 25 = 198$, which is ₹ 198. Option (c) uses the diameter as the radius, option (d) paints the two ends as well, and option (a) multiplies the volume by the rate.

questions.stem_md: A solid steel ball of radius $3$ cm is melted and recast into identical small balls of radius $1$ cm. The number of small balls obtained is
questions.solution_md: Volume does not change: $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 3^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 1^3$, so $n = 27$. Option (d) divides the radii squared (areas), and option (a) divides the radii only.

questions.stem_md: A solid metal cylinder of base radius $6$ cm and height $9$ cm is melted and recast into a solid cone with the same base radius. The height of the cone is
questions.solution_md: Equal volumes: $\pi \times 6^2 \times 9 = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 6^2 \times h$, so $h = 3 \times 9 = 27$ cm. Option (a) forgets the $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the cone, which would give the cylinder's own height.

questions.stem_md: A solid pencil-sharpener model is a cylinder of radius $3.5$ cm and height $10$ cm with a cone of the same radius and vertical height $12$ cm fixed on its upper end. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, the area of its outside surface (the lower end is flat and exposed) is
questions.solution_md: The cone has $l = 12.5$ cm. Outside area $=$ lower end $+$ curved cylinder $+$ curved cone $= \pi \times 3.5^2 + 2\pi \times 3.5 \times 10 + \pi \times 3.5 \times 12.5 = 126\pi = 396$ cm$^2$. Option (b) counts the upper circular face of the cylinder, which is covered by the cone; option (c) uses $12$ instead of the slant height; option (d) leaves out the flat lower end.

questions.stem_md: The radius of a spherical balloon is increased by $10\%$. The percentage increase in its surface area is
questions.solution_md: Area $= 4\pi r^2$ grows with the square of the radius, so the new area is $1.1^2 = 1.21$ times the old one, an increase of $21\%$. Option (a) is the increase in volume, which grows with the cube: $1.1^3 = 1.331$.

**Assertion (A):** The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius $r$ is $2\pi r^2$.

**Reason (R):** A solid hemisphere has one curved surface and one flat circular face.

**Reason (R):** The surface area of a sphere of radius $r$ is $4\pi r^2$.

**Assertion (A):** A cylindrical tank of radius $0.5$ m and height $1.4$ m holds $1100$ litres of water (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).

**Reason (R):** One cubic metre is equal to $100$ litres.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A hemisphere of radius $r$ is fixed on one flat end of a cylinder of radius $r$. The surface area of the solid is less than the sum of the surface areas of the cylinder and the hemisphere taken separately.

**Reason (R):** The circular faces where the two solids are joined are no longer on the outside of the solid.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: the joined faces, one of area $\pi r^2$ on the cylinder and one of area $\pi r^2$ on the hemisphere, are hidden, so the outside area drops by $2\pi r^2$.

questions.stem_md: If both the radius and the height of a cylindrical oil can are doubled, the area of its curved surface becomes four times as large.
questions.solution_md: The curved area $2\pi r h$ becomes $2\pi (2r)(2h) = 4 \times 2\pi r h$, so it is four times as large.

questions.stem_md: A student measures a solid wooden cone and finds a base radius of $9$ cm and a vertical height of $12$ cm. She then claims that the sloping edge from the apex to the rim of the base is $21$ cm long.
questions.solution_md: False: $l = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm. The value $21$ is $r + h$, but the sloping edge is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, so it is shorter than the sum of the two other sides.

questions.stem_md: The surface area of a sphere is exactly four times the area of the great circle that cuts it in half.
questions.solution_md: True: the great circle has area $\pi r^2$ and the sphere has surface area $4\pi r^2$, which is four times as large.

questions.stem_md: When a solid is melted and recast into another solid, the total surface area stays the same as before.
questions.solution_md: False: it is the volume that stays the same. For example, one sphere of radius $3$ cm recast into $27$ spheres of radius $1$ cm has the same volume, but its surface area $36\pi$ cm$^2$ becomes $27 \times 4\pi = 108\pi$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A solid sphere is melted and recast into $8$ equal small spheres. The radius of each small sphere is one-eighth of the radius of the original sphere.
questions.solution_md: False: $8 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r_1^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ gives $r_1^3 = \dfrac{r^3}{8}$, so $r_1 = \dfrac{r}{2}$, half of the original radius.

questions.stem_md: A solid cylindrical wax candle has radius $3.5$ cm and height $8$ cm. Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$, its volume is ___ cm$^3$.
A conical lampshade has base radius $12$ cm and vertical height $16$ cm, so its slant height is ___ cm.
A solid brass paperweight is a hemisphere of radius $14$ cm resting on its flat face. Counting that flat face too, the area of its entire outside is ___ cm$^2$ (take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$).
questions.solution_md: $S = 3 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 1848$ cm$^2$, which is the curved part $1232$ plus the flat face $616$.

questions.stem_md: A rainwater tank in a housing society holds $6.6$ cubic metres of water. Since one cubic metre is $1000$ litres, the tank holds ___ litres.
questions.solution_md: $6.6 \times 1000 = 6600$ litres.

questions.solution_md: In one revolution the roller covers its curved surface: $r = 0.35$ m, so $S = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.35 \times 1.2 = 2.64$ m$^2$. For $150$ revolutions: $2.64 \times 150 = 396$.

questions.solution_md: $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^2 \times 36 = 4158$ cm$^3$.

A solid metal sphere of radius $6$ cm is drawn into a uniform wire of diameter $4$ mm. Find the length of the wire in metres.
questions.solution_md: The wire is a cylinder of radius $0.2$ cm. Equal volumes: $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 6^3 = \pi \times 0.2^2 \times l$, so $288 = 0.04 \times l$ and $l = \dfrac{288}{0.04} = 7200$ cm. In metres: $\dfrac{7200}{100} = 72$.

questions.stem_md: A cylindrical jar for sweets has base radius $4.2$ cm and height $6.2$ cm. A hemispherical dome of the same radius covers its top, and the space inside the dome belongs to the jar. Find the total capacity in cm$^3$. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
The curved surface area of a solid cylindrical pillar model is $308$ cm$^2$ and its base radius is $3.5$ cm. Find its height and its volume. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 3.5 \times h = 308$ gives $22 \times h = 308$, so $h = \dfrac{308}{22} = 14$ cm.

$V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 3.5^2 \times 14 = 539$ cm$^3$.

questions.stem_md: A paper cone for roasted peanuts, sold on a beach in Puri, has base radius $9$ cm and vertical height $12$ cm. Find its slant height and its curved surface area, leaving the area in terms of $\pi$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$l = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm.

$S = \pi \times 9 \times 15 = 135\pi$, so the curved surface area is $135\pi$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A hemispherical steel bowl in a canteen has an inside diameter of $28$ cm. Find the area of its inner curved surface. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Inner radius $= \dfrac{28}{2} = 14$ cm.

Inner curved area $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 1232$ cm$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A craftsman melts one solid silver ball of radius $3$ cm to make tiny beads, each a solid sphere of radius $0.5$ cm. How many beads does he get?

answer.model_answer_md:
Volume of the ball $=$ number of beads $\times$ volume of one bead: $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 3^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 0.5^3$.

$n = \dfrac{3^3}{0.5^3} = \dfrac{27}{0.125} = 216$ beads.

questions.solution_md: Equate the volumes; the common factor $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi$ cancels.

questions.stem_md: A copper tube in a chemistry laboratory is $35$ cm long. Its outer radius is $7$ cm and the wall is $1.4$ cm thick. Find the volume of copper in the tube. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Inner radius $= 7 - 1.4 = 5.6$ cm.

Volume of copper $=$ outer cylinder $-$ inner cylinder $= \pi h (R^2 - r^2)$.

$V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 \times (7^2 - 5.6^2) = 1940.4$ cm$^3$.

questions.solution_md: Subtract the wall thickness from the outer radius before using the difference of the two circular areas.

questions.stem_md: A conical juice dispenser at a fair in Jodhpur has a base radius of $14$ cm and a vertical height of $48$ cm. How many litres of juice does it hold when full? Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ and $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm$^3$.

questions.stem_md: A solid hemispherical brass bell of radius $14$ cm is to be gold-plated all over, including its flat base, at ₹ $1.25$ per cm$^2$. Find the cost of plating. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Whole surface of a solid hemisphere $= 3\pi r^2$: $S = 3 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14^2 = 1848$ cm$^2$.

Cost $= 1848 \times 1.25 = 2310$, so the plating costs ₹ 2310.

questions.stem_md: A solid metal cone with base radius $12$ cm is melted and recast into a solid sphere of radius $6$ cm. Find the height of the cone.

answer.model_answer_md:
Volume of the sphere $= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 6^3 = 288\pi$.

Volume of the cone $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 12^2 \times h = 48\pi h$.

$48\pi h = 288\pi$, so $h = \dfrac{288}{48} = 6$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The volume does not change when a solid is melted and recast.

questions.stem_md: A garden ornament is a solid hemisphere of radius $10.5$ cm with a solid cone of the same radius and vertical height $36$ cm fixed on its flat face. Find its total volume. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Hemisphere: $V_1 = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^3 = 2425.5$ cm$^3$.

Cone: $V_2 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^2 \times 36 = 4158$ cm$^3$.

Total volume $= 2425.5 + 4158 = 6583.5$ cm$^3$.

questions.solution_md: The flat faces are joined, so the volumes simply add.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: A solid metal ball of radius $6$ cm is completely submerged in water in an upright cylindrical vessel of radius $12$ cm; no water spills. By how many centimetres does the water level rise?

answer.model_answer_md:
The water that rises is a cylinder of radius $12$ cm and height $x$ cm, with the same volume as the ball.

Volume of the ball: $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 6^3 = 288\pi$ cm$^3$.

Rise in the vessel: $\pi \times 12^2 \times x = 144\pi x$.

$144\pi x = 288\pi$, so $x = \dfrac{288}{144} = 2$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A solid iron sphere of radius $9$ cm is melted and drawn into a solid cylindrical rod of radius $4.5$ cm. Find the length of the rod.

answer.model_answer_md:
Volume of the sphere $= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 9^3 = 972\pi$ cm$^3$.

Volume of the rod $= \pi \times 4.5^2 \times l = 20.25\pi l$.

$20.25\pi l = 972\pi$, so $l = \dfrac{972}{20.25} = 48$.

The rod is $48$ cm long.

Lower base: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^2 = 13.86$. Curved cylinder: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1 \times 8 = 105.6$. Curved hemisphere: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^2 = 27.72$.

Total surface area $= 13.86 + 105.6 + 27.72 = 147.18$ cm$^2$.

(ii) Cylinder: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^2 \times 8 = 110.88$. Hemisphere: $\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^3 = 19.404$. Volume $= 110.88 + 19.404 = 130.284$ cm$^3$.

questions.stem_md: A steel pipe in a water-works yard in Nagpur is $21$ cm long, with an external diameter of $8$ cm and a wall $1$ cm thick. Find (i) the volume of steel and (ii) its mass in grams, if $1$ cm$^3$ of this steel has a mass of $8$ g. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
External radius $R = 4$ cm; internal radius $r = 4 - 1 = 3$ cm.

(i) $V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 \times (4^2 - 3^2) = 462$ cm$^3$.

(ii) Mass $= 462 \times 8 = 3696$ g.

questions.solution_md: Work out the radii from the diameter and the wall, then the volume between the two cylinders.

questions.stem_md:
An open cylindrical water tank at a hostel in Dehradun has an inner radius of $2.1$ m and a depth of $3$ m. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ and $1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres. Show all working.

(a) Find the capacity of the tank in litres.

(b) Find the area of the metal sheet needed to make the tank, which has a base but no lid.

(c) Find the cost of the sheet at ₹ $150$ per m$^2$, and the time to fill the empty tank with a pump that delivers $3465$ litres per minute.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $V = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^2 \times 3 = 41.58$ m$^3$. In litres: $41.58 \times 1000 = 41580$ litres.

(b) Sheet $=$ curved surface $+$ base, because the top is open.

Curved surface: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1 \times 3 = 39.6$ m$^2$. Base: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^2 = 13.86$ m$^2$. Sheet $= 39.6 + 13.86 = 53.46$ m$^2$.

(c) Cost $= 53.46 \times 150 = 8019$, that is ₹ 8019.

Time $= \dfrac{41580}{3465} = 12$ minutes.

questions.solution_md: Capacity from the volume; sheet from the curved surface plus the base only; then cost and time.

questions.stem_md:
A heap of wheat in a mandi near Hapur is in the shape of a cone with base radius $2.1$ m and vertical height $7.2$ m. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$. Show all working.

(a) Find the slant height of the heap and the area of its curved surface.

(b) Find the volume of wheat in the heap.

(c) The heap is covered by a tarpaulin that costs ₹ $36$ per m$^2$; find the cost of the tarpaulin for the curved surface. Also find the mass of the heap in kilograms if $1$ m$^3$ of wheat has a mass of $750$ kg.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $l = \sqrt{2.1^2 + 7.2^2} = \sqrt{56.25} = 7.5$ m.

Curved surface: $S = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1 \times 7.5 = 49.5$ m$^2$.

(b) $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.1^2 \times 7.2 = 33.264$ m$^3$.

(c) Cost of the tarpaulin $= 49.5 \times 36 = 1782$, that is ₹ 1782.

Mass $= 33.264 \times 750 = 24948$ kg.

questions.solution_md: Slant height first, then area, volume, cost and mass in that order.

questions.stem_md:
A hollow iron sphere has an outer radius of $9$ cm and an inner radius of $6$ cm. Show all working.

(a) Find the volume of iron in the shell, leaving the answer in terms of $\pi$.

(b) The shell is melted and recast into solid spheres of radius $3$ cm. How many spheres are made?

(c) The outer surface of the original sphere is chrome-plated at ₹ $0.25$ per cm$^2$. Find the cost of plating. Take $\pi = 3.14$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Volume of iron $= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (R^3 - r^3)$, so $V = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times (9^3 - 6^3) = 684\pi$ cm$^3$.

(b) One small sphere: $\dfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 3^3 = 36\pi$ cm$^3$. Number $= \dfrac{684\pi}{36\pi} = 19$ spheres.

(c) Outer surface area $= 4 \times 3.14 \times 9^2 = 1017.36$ cm$^2$.

Cost $= 1017.36 \times 0.25 = 254.34$, that is ₹ 254.34.

questions.solution_md: Volume of the shell is the outer sphere minus the inner sphere; the plating needs only the outer surface.

questions.stem_md:
A solid metal cylinder of a foundry in Rajkot has base radius $6$ cm and height $12$ cm. It is melted and recast into small solid spheres, each of radius $3$ cm. Show all working and leave answers in terms of $\pi$ where needed.

(a) Find the volume of the cylinder.

(b) Find the volume of one small sphere.

(c) Find the number of spheres made. Then compare the total surface area of all the spheres with the total surface area of the cylinder, writing the first as a multiple of the second.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $V = \pi \times 6^2 \times 12 = 432\pi$ cm$^3$.

(b) $v = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 3^3 = 36\pi$ cm$^3$.

(c) Number of spheres $= \dfrac{432\pi}{36\pi} = 12$.

Surface area of the cylinder: $2\pi \times 6 \times (6 + 12) = 216\pi$ cm$^2$.

Total surface area of the spheres: $12 \times 4\pi \times 3^2 = 432\pi$ cm$^2$. Since $\dfrac{432\pi}{216\pi} = 2$, the spheres have twice the surface area of the cylinder.

questions.solution_md: Melting keeps the volume and changes the surface area.

questions.stem_md:
A cylindrical tub at a hardware shop in Ludhiana has an inner radius of $6$ cm and is $20$ cm tall. It holds water to a depth of $9$ cm. Solid steel balls, each of radius $3$ cm, are dropped one by one into the tub, and each sinks completely. Show all working and leave volumes in terms of $\pi$.

(a) Find the volume of one ball.

(b) Eight balls are dropped in. Find the rise in the water level and the new depth.

(c) How many more balls can be dropped before the water just reaches the brim? What volume of water overflows if one more ball than that is dropped?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $v = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 3^3 = 36\pi$ cm$^3$.

(b) The water that rises is a cylinder of radius $6$ cm: its volume for a rise of $x$ cm is $\pi \times 6^2 \times x = 36\pi x$.

Eight balls: $8 \times 36\pi = 288\pi$, so $36\pi x = 288\pi$ and $x = \dfrac{288}{36} = 8$ cm.

New depth $= 9 + 8 = 17$ cm.

(c) The brim is at $20$ cm, so the water can rise a further $20 - 17 = 3$ cm. Each ball raises the water by $\dfrac{36\pi}{36\pi} = 1$ cm, so $3$ more balls just fill the tub to the brim.

One more ball than that overflows its own volume: $36\pi$ cm$^3$.

questions.solution_md: Each ball has the same volume as a $1$ cm slice of water in this tub, so the rise per ball is $1$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
A decorative solid in a garden at Udaipur is made of three parts joined along their circular faces: a hemisphere at the bottom, a cylinder of height $20$ cm in the middle and a cone of vertical height $14$ cm on top. All three have radius $10.5$ cm. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$. Show all working.

(a) Find the slant height of the cone and the total outside surface area of the solid.

(b) Find the volume of the solid.

(c) The outside is painted at ₹ $0.40$ per cm$^2$. Find the cost of painting, and write the volume of the solid in litres.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $l = \sqrt{10.5^2 + 14^2} = \sqrt{306.25} = 17.5$ cm.

The joined faces are hidden, so the outside surface is the curved hemisphere, the curved cylinder and the curved cone.

Hemisphere: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^2 = 693$. Cylinder: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5 \times 20 = 1320$. Cone: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5 \times 17.5 = 577.5$.

Total surface area $= 693 + 1320 + 577.5 = 2590.5$ cm$^2$.

(b) Hemisphere: $\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^3 = 2425.5$. Cylinder: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^2 \times 20 = 6930$. Cone: $\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5^2 \times 14 = 1617$.

Volume $= 2425.5 + 6930 + 1617 = 10972.5$ cm$^3$.

(c) Cost $= 2590.5 \times 0.4 = 1036.2$, that is ₹ 1036.2.

In litres: $\dfrac{10972.5}{1000} = 10.9725$ litres.

questions.solution_md: Three joined parts: outside areas of the curved surfaces only, volumes of all three parts.

questions.stem_md:
A stone bird-bath in a park in Bhopal starts as a solid cylinder of radius $21$ cm and height $30$ cm. A hemispherical hollow of radius $21$ cm is then carved out of the top face. Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$. Show all working.

(a) Find the volume of stone left in the bird-bath.

(b) Find the total surface area of the bird-bath, including its base and the hollow.

(c) The whole surface is polished at ₹ $0.05$ per cm$^2$, and the stone has a mass of $2.5$ g per cm$^3$. Find the cost of polishing and the mass of the bird-bath in kilograms.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Cylinder: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 21^2 \times 30 = 41580$ cm$^3$. Hollow hemisphere: $\dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21^3 = 19404$ cm$^3$.

Stone left $= 41580 - 19404 = 22176$ cm$^3$.

(b) The hollow has the same radius as the cylinder, so the top face disappears completely. The surfaces are the curved cylinder, the base and the inside of the hollow.

Curved cylinder: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 \times 30 = 3960$. Base: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 21^2 = 1386$. Hollow: $2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21^2 = 2772$.

Total surface area $= 3960 + 1386 + 2772 = 8118$ cm$^2$.

(c) Cost $= 8118 \times 0.05 = 405.9$, that is ₹ 405.9.

Mass $= 22176 \times 2.5 = 55440$ g $= \dfrac{55440}{1000} = 55.44$ kg.

questions.solution_md: The hollow takes away the top face and adds a hemispherical surface; polish cost uses areas and mass uses the volume of stone left.
